sections.title: Understanding Highly Complex Multi-Graph Analysis
sections.content: In Level 3, 3–4 graphs (Scatter Plot, Line Graph, Bar Graph, Table) are given together. Questions are not solved by direct calculation alone but rely on logic, trend analysis, and conditions. The solution typically has 4–6 steps: Step 1 – Analyze each graph independently, Step 2 – Identify variables, Step 3 – Establish a baseline, Step 4 – Apply conditions, Step 5 – Calculate the new value, Step 6 – Perform comparison or optimization.

sections.title: Linking Scatter Plot with Cumulative Line Graph
sections.content: A Scatter Plot shows trends or correlation, such as the relationship between sales and advertising expenditure. A Line Graph may show cumulative growth. First identify the estimated slope or trend from the Scatter Plot. Then calculate the cumulative value from the Line Graph. Example strategy: (1) Take the estimated growth rate from the Scatter Plot, (2) Apply it to the base value from the Line Graph, (3) Calculate the new projected total.

sections.title: Regression Logic and Trend Estimation
sections.content: If the points in a Scatter Plot form an almost straight line, calculate the average increase per unit. Example: When spending increases by ₹10,000, sales increase by 500 units. If the Line Graph shows that spending will increase by ₹30,000 next year, the estimated increase = 3 × 500 = 1,500 units. This estimate is then combined with cumulative data.

sections.title: Multi-variable Optimization
sections.content: Graph 1 shows cost changes. Graph 2 shows the production limit (volume cap). Graph 3 shows tax slabs. Solution order: (1) Calculate cost per unit, (2) Apply the maximum production limit, (3) Calculate gross profit, (4) Deduct tax according to the tax slab, (5) Compare net profit, (6) Identify the point of maximum profit. Checking boundary conditions is essential.

sections.title: Dynamic Baseline and Compound Iterations
sections.content: Sometimes the output of Graph 1 becomes the input of Graph 2. Example: A Line Graph shows 10% annual growth. A Bar Graph shows next year's production based on the increased value. Solution: (1) Take Year 1 as the base, (2) Apply 10% growth, (3) Make the new value the base for Year 2, (4) Apply the next percentage, (5) Calculate the final cumulative result.

sections.title: Deep Conditional Swapping Logic
sections.content: If data of Year X from Graph 1 is swapped with Graph 2, first calculate the original averages of both. Then apply the swap. Step 1 – Identify values of Year X and Y in both graphs. Step 2 – Swap them. Step 3 – Calculate the new total. Step 4 – Calculate the new average. Step 5 – Compare the minimum average.

sections.title: Boundary Conditions and Extreme Cases
sections.content: In optimization questions, maximum or minimum values are often found at boundaries. Example: If maximum production is 5,000 units, check profit at both 5,000 and 0 units. Analyze intermediate values based on trends.

sections.title: Massive Data Synthesis Strategy
sections.content: 1. Summarize all data into one table. 2. Convert all values into the same units. 3. Convert percentages into actual values. 4. Apply logic step by step. 5. Finally compare and conclude. In Level 3, structured thinking is the most important skill.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Adding compound growth instead of multiplying. 2. Applying tax slabs incorrectly. 3. Using the old average after swapping values. 4. Forgetting to check boundary conditions. 5. Assuming scatter trends without calculating averages.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 3 Mixed DI usually involves 4–6 steps. Trend analysis, multi-variable linking, compound growth, and conditional changes are key elements. Always calculate intermediate values clearly and check optimization at the end.

tricks.title: Compound Growth Shortcut
tricks.explanation: Convert consecutive growth percentages into multiplication.

tricks.title: Identify Trend per Unit
tricks.explanation: Difference between two points / difference in input.
tricks.example: ₹20,000 increase leads to 1,000 units increase → 50 units per ₹1,000

tricks.title: Apply Tax Slabs Quickly
tricks.explanation: First calculate gross profit, then apply tax in parts according to slabs.
tricks.example: ₹5,00,000 profit: 10% on first ₹2,00,000, 20% on the remaining

tricks.title: Swapping Trick
tricks.explanation: New total after swap = Old total − X + Y.

tricks.title: Check Optimization Boundaries
tricks.explanation: Always test minimum and maximum limits.
tricks.example: Compare profit at 0 units and 5,000 units

tricks.title: Dynamic Baseline Trick
tricks.explanation: Each year’s new base = previous year’s final value.

tricks.title: Advanced Weighted ROI
tricks.explanation: Total profit / total investment across different years.

tricks.title: Convert Data into a Unified Table
tricks.explanation: Write all graph values in one place.
tricks.example: Year-wise cost, production, and tax in one table

tricks.title: Correlation Indicator
tricks.explanation: Upward scatter trend → positive correlation; downward → negative.
tricks.example: Advertising increases, sales increase → positive trend

tricks.title: Massive Calculation Control
tricks.explanation: Estimate first in large numbers, then calculate precisely.
